title: Names that break software: NULL, True and little Bobby Tables
description: A man picks the licence plate NULL and ends up with $12,049 in strangers' parking fines. A woman named Null can't book a flight online. An actor named True gets locked out of iCloud for six months. A whole English town can't sign up for AOL. Each Question starts with a real person or place, asks what the software got wrong, and ends with the fix.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: In late 2016, a security researcher registered this California vanity plate as a programmer's joke. What did it bring him?
questions.description: Joseph Tartaro, known as Droogie, chose `NULL` because in many programming languages it means "no value".

images.alt: A plain, generic licence plate with the word NULL in large capitals and the small label vanity plate underneath.
images.caption: Generic illustration, not California's plate design. Image: Quizbun.

images.alt: Two rows of three boxes. Top row, labelled bug, blank plate saved as the text NULL: a parking ticket for a Honda with the plate left blank becomes a citation record with plate equal to the string NULL, and the owner lookup finds NULL equals NULL, a match, so the fine goes to the owner of the NULL plate. Bottom row, labelled fix, blank plate saved as a real NULL: the same ticket becomes a record with plate equal to NULL, no value at all, and the lookup NULL equals the string NULL gives unknown, so there is no match and the ticket is sent for review.
images.caption: Simplified reconstruction of the reported mechanism. Diagram: Quizbun.

options.text: Parking tickets written without a plate number were matched to his car, so strangers' fines were mailed to him
Plate-reading cameras skipped his car, so he never got a ticket again
The DMV system crashed each time an officer searched for his plate
Nothing: the DMV rejected the plate as a reserved word before it was issued

questions.explanation:
Hundreds of tickets for Hondas, Toyotas and Mercedes arrived from all over California. He drives an Infiniti, and he says some of the tickets dated from 2014, before he even had the plate.

The tickets came through the Citation Processing Center, a private company that handles tickets for many California cities. When an officer left the plate field empty, the record reportedly stored `NULL` as text. To a database, the four letters N-U-L-L are an ordinary string, and they match a real plate that reads `NULL`. So every ticket without a plate matched his car.

Cameras play no part here. The officer left the plate field empty, and the system stored that empty field the wrong way.
questions.references: [WIRED: How a 'NULL' License Plate Landed One Hacker in Ticket Hell (2019)](https://www.wired.com/story/null-license-plate-landed-one-hacker-ticket-hell/), [Gizmodo: Security researcher's 'NULL' vanity plates cause glitch](https://gizmodo.com/security-researcher-s-null-vanity-plates-cause-glitch-1837206261)

questions.title: At the peak, how much in other people's fines was charged to the NULL plate, in US dollars?
questions.description: Type a number. Anything within about $1,000 counts.
questions.explanation:
WIRED reported that at one point he faced **$12,049** in fines that weren't his. Most tickets were $37 to $80 each, for parking and stopping violations, so that's well over a hundred tickets.

The DMV and the processing company cancelled most of them, and by his DEF CON talk in August 2019 the total was down to $6,262. New tickets kept coming, though. Cancelling fines cleans up the data but leaves the bug in place, so every new ticket without a plate still matched his car.
questions.references: [WIRED: How a 'NULL' License Plate Landed One Hacker in Ticket Hell (2019)](https://www.wired.com/story/null-license-plate-landed-one-hacker-ticket-hell/)

questions.title: For more than a year, the plate caused no trouble. What set off the flood of tickets?

options.text: He paid a genuine $35 ticket in early 2018, which linked the plate NULL to his name and address
He renewed his registration online in 2017, and the DMV website rejected his plate
He gave a talk about the plate at DEF CON, and someone reported him
A new plate-reading camera network came online in Los Angeles

questions.explanation:
In early 2018 he got a real ticket, $35 for a missing registration sticker, and paid it. According to WIRED, the payment seems to have linked `NULL` to his name and address in the processing center's database. From then on, every ticket stored with a `NULL` plate had somewhere to go.

The 2017 renewal was a real early warning. The DMV website said his plate and VIN were invalid, and he renewed with a reference number instead. That bug lived in a website form, though, and didn't touch the ticket system. The DEF CON talk came in 2019, long after the tickets started.

Bugs like this are common. Bad data can sit unnoticed for a long time until another record gives it something to join with.
questions.references: [WIRED: How a 'NULL' License Plate Landed One Hacker in Ticket Hell (2019)](https://www.wired.com/story/null-license-plate-landed-one-hacker-ticket-hell/)

questions.title: Which changes to the ticket system would stop tickets with no plate from reaching the NULL driver?

options.text: Store a missing plate as SQL `NULL`, not as the text `'NULL'`
Refuse to look up an owner when the plate is missing, and send the ticket for manual review
Replace the text `'NULL'` with a different placeholder, such as `'NONE'`
Compare plates case-sensitively, so `'NULL'` no longer matches `'null'`

questions.explanation:
SQL `NULL` means "no value", and it never equals anything, not even another `NULL`. When `plate` is a real `NULL`, the comparison `plate = 'NULL'` returns *unknown*, and a `WHERE` clause keeps only rows where the condition is true. So a real `NULL` can't match anybody.

```sql
-- The bug: a missing plate stored as a four-letter string
SELECT owner FROM plates WHERE plate = 'NULL';   -- finds the NULL driver

-- The fix: store no value, then check for it explicitly
SELECT * FROM citations WHERE plate IS NULL;     -- the tickets that need review
```

The second fix is a safety net. If the plate is empty, the code skips the owner lookup and a person reviews the ticket.

A new placeholder just moves the problem. Plates such as `NONE`, `NOPLATE` or `MISSING` are just as easy to register, and whoever gets one inherits the bug. Case-sensitive matching doesn't help either, because the plate and the placeholder are both uppercase `NULL`.

The SQL query detective Quiz covers how `NULL` behaves in comparisons, joins and aggregates.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Null (SQL)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Null_(SQL)), [WIRED: How a 'NULL' License Plate Landed One Hacker in Ticket Hell (2019)](https://www.wired.com/story/null-license-plate-landed-one-hacker-ticket-hell/)

questions.title: Jennifer Null from Virginia tries to book a flight online. What happens on most airline websites?

options.text: The site says she left the surname field blank and asks her to try again
The booking goes through, but her ticket prints with no name on it
The site flags her as a possible security threat and blocks the booking
The site charges her card and then loses the booking

questions.explanation:
She told the BBC in 2016 that most sites say she left the surname field empty. She has to phone the airline instead, and she's sometimes been told her story can't be true.

The likely cause is a check that treats the text `"Null"` as "no value". Some code turns a missing value into the string `"null"` when it serializes data, so a later check that sees `"null"` can't tell an empty field from her real surname.

It's the NULL plate bug in reverse. The ticket system turned missing data into a name, and airline sites turn her name into missing data.
questions.references: [BBC Future: Hello, I'm Mr Null. My name makes me invisible to computers (2016)](https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20160325-the-names-that-break-computer-systems)

questions.title: In March 2021, actor and author Rachel True said she'd been locked out of her iCloud account. How long had it been going on?

options.text: About six months
About two days
About two weeks
About three years

questions.explanation:
Rachel True, known for the 1996 film *The Craft*, said she hadn't been able to use iCloud for about **six months**. She'd spent more than six hours on the phone with support over several days, and Apple kept charging her for storage she couldn't reach.

After she posted the error message she kept seeing, the story went viral and a member of the iCloud team offered to help. The next Question looks at that message.
questions.references: [The Register: Name True, iCloud access false (2021)](https://www.theregister.com/2021/03/08/name_true_apple_icloud_access/), [9to5Mac: iCloud coding error locks out Rachel True over a boolean flag (2021)](https://9to5mac.com/2021/03/07/icloud-user-locked-out-for-six-months-over-coding-bug-related-to-her-last-name/)

questions.title: Rachel True's error message read: `Type error: cannot set value 'true' to property 'lastName'`. What does it suggest went wrong?

images.alt: A three-step flow. A form field labelled last name contains True. Read without quotes, it becomes lastName colon true in lowercase, a boolean. A schema check that expects lastName to be a string then raises a type error. Below, two boxes compare the quoted string True, her surname as text, with the bare boolean true, a yes or no value that is not a name.
images.caption: Illustrative. Apple has not published the cause. Diagram: Quizbun.

options.text: Somewhere, her surname was read as the boolean `true`, and the `lastName` field only accepts strings
Her surname was on a blocklist of reserved words, and the account was frozen
Her surname was too short to meet a minimum length rule
Her surname matched a SQL keyword and was treated as an injection attempt

questions.explanation:
The message names the field, `lastName`, and the value, a lowercase `true`, which is a boolean. Somewhere between her keyboard and Apple's servers, a parser or converter saw the four letters without quotes and turned them into a yes/no value. The next step expected a string and rejected the boolean.

The fix is to keep text as text the whole way through. Send names as quoted JSON strings, declare the field as a string in the schema, and never let a generic converter guess a type from how a value looks.

Apple didn't publish a post-mortem, so this explanation comes from the error message alone. The other Options don't fit that message. A blocklist, a length rule or an injection filter would reject the name itself. None of them would complain that a `true` value can't go into a text field.
questions.references: [The Register: Name True, iCloud access false (2021)](https://www.theregister.com/2021/03/08/name_true_apple_icloud_access/), [Engadget: iCloud allegedly locked out a user over her last name (2021)](https://www.engadget.com/icloud-true-last-name-lock-out-192224309.html)

questions.title: A YAML config file lists country codes. A YAML 1.1 parser such as PyYAML loads the list below. What does Norway's `NO` become?
questions.description:
```yaml
countries:
  - GB
  - FR
  - NO
```

Type the value as the parser would print it.
questions.explanation:
YAML 1.1 reads a bare `NO` as the boolean **false**. Its type repository lists `y`, `Y`, `yes`, `Yes`, `YES`, `on`, `On`, `ON` and the `true` spellings as true, and `n`, `N`, `no`, `No`, `NO`, `off`, `Off`, `OFF` and the `false` spellings as false. So the list loads as `['GB', 'FR', False]`, and Norway disappears. Developers call this the Norway problem.

YAML 1.2 (2009) narrowed its core schema to `true` and `false`, but many popular parsers, including PyYAML, still follow 1.1.

The fix is the same as for Rachel True: mark it as text. Write `"NO"` in quotes, or use a parser mode or schema that loads strings as strings.

questions.title: In 1996, people in Scunthorpe, an English town in North Lincolnshire, couldn't sign up for AOL. Why?

images.alt: Two panels using the harmless example word hell and the village name Hellifield. The substring check, name to lower case includes hell, highlights the first four letters of Hellifield and blocks it. The whole-word check, a regular expression with word boundaries around hell, allows Hellifield because hell is only part of a longer word.
images.caption: The same mechanism shown with a milder word. Diagram: Quizbun.

options.text: AOL's profanity filter found a rude word hidden inside the town's name
AOL didn't yet offer service to that part of England
The town's name was longer than AOL's address field allowed
The town's dial-up exchange wasn't compatible with AOL's modems

questions.explanation:
AOL's filter looked for banned words *anywhere* in the text, and one hides in letters two to five of "Scunthorpe". A substring check doesn't know where words start or end, so it blocked the whole town.

The diagram uses a milder word. Hellifield, a village in North Yorkshire, contains `hell`, so a substring filter for `hell` blocks it too.

This case gave the bug its name. When a filter blocks innocent text because of a hidden substring, that's the **Scunthorpe problem**. Penistone, Clitheroe and London's Horniman Museum have all run into it too.

questions.title: AOL's first response didn't fix the filter. What did it tell Scunthorpe residents to do?

options.text: Enter the town as "Sconthorpe"
Enter a nearby town's name instead
Write to AOL for a manual exemption
Leave the town field blank

questions.explanation:
Resident Doug Blackie found that AOL would register him only if he typed the town as **Sconthorpe**. Changing one letter hid the banned substring. The *Scunthorpe Evening Telegraph* covered it on 9 April 1996, and RISKS Digest summed it up: as far as AOL was concerned, the town would "henceforth be known as" Sconthorpe.

This workaround changes the user's data to suit the filter, so the next town or surname with a hidden match hits the same bug. AOL did the same to Craig Cockburn, whose surname contains a banned word. At first it told him to replace the first "o" with a zero.

questions.title: A developer switches the profanity filter from substring matching to whole-word matching, like `\bword\b`. Which problems remain?

options.text: A person whose surname is itself a word on the list is still blocked
Anyone who adds spaces, dots or digits inside a banned word gets past the filter
Languages written without spaces between words, such as Chinese, Japanese and Thai, have no word boundaries for `\b` to find
Scunthorpe is still blocked

questions.explanation:
Whole-word matching fixes Scunthorpe itself. In a regular expression, `\b` matches only at the edge of a word, so a banned word buried inside "Scunthorpe" no longer matches.

Three problems remain:

- **Names that are on the list.** Some surnames are also English words that a filter might ban. Whole-word matching blocks them just as before.
- **Evasion.** Put spaces, dots or digits between the letters of a rude word and it isn't a whole word anymore, so it gets through.
- **Scripts without spaces.** In JavaScript, `\b` treats only ASCII letters, digits and `_` as word characters, and Chinese, Japanese and Thai don't put spaces between words. The filter either matches inside other words again or matches nothing at all.

A filter can't tell what a name means. For names and places, it's safer to skip automatic blocking and send doubtful cases to a person.

questions.title: In xkcd's "Exploits of a Mom", a school loses its whole student table because of one pupil's name. Which changes would stop this from happening again?
questions.description:
A mother named her son `Robert'); DROP TABLE Students;--`, or little Bobby Tables for short. The school's code builds its query like this:

```js
db.query("INSERT INTO Students (name) VALUES ('" + name + "');");
```

options.text: Use a prepared statement and pass the name as a bound parameter
Use the ORM's normal insert method, which binds values as parameters
Remove apostrophes from every name before building the query
Reject any name that contains the word `DROP`

questions.explanation:
Pasted into the query, the name closes the string with `')`, ends the statement with `;`, adds its own `DROP TABLE Students;` and comments out the rest with `--`. The database can't tell the school's SQL from the pupil's name, because they arrive as one piece of text.

A bound parameter sends the SQL and the value separately:

```js
db.query("INSERT INTO Students (name) VALUES (?)", [name]);
```

The database parses the query first, then treats `name` as data, whatever characters it contains. An ORM's normal methods do the same thing under the hood. OWASP lists parameterized queries as the first defence against SQL injection.

Stripping apostrophes breaks real names such as O'Brien. It also misses injections that need no quote at all, such as a query built as `"... WHERE id = " + id`. Banning `DROP` is a word filter with the Scunthorpe problem both ways. It blocks harmless text that contains "drop", and an attacker can still delete or read data with other statements.
questions.references: [xkcd 327: Exploits of a Mom](https://xkcd.com/327/), [OWASP: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)

questions.title: In June 2010, Patrick McKenzie published "Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names". How many falsehoods are on the list?
questions.explanation:
The list has **40** numbered items. It opens with "People have exactly one canonical full name" and ends with "People have names." The items get more exasperated as it goes, and several come in escalating runs, such as a name being assigned at birth, then within a year, then within five years.

Each item is an assumption that real software makes, and each one is wrong for someone. The post started a whole genre, and there are now "Falsehoods programmers believe" lists for time, addresses, phone numbers and email.
questions.references: [Patrick McKenzie: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names (2010)](https://www.kalzumeus.com/2010/06/17/falsehoods-programmers-believe-about-names/)

questions.title: McKenzie's post opens by pointing to another programmer's complaint from the same day. What happened to John Graham-Cumming?

options.text: A website told him his last name contained invalid characters, because of the hyphen
A bank merged his account with another customer who had the same name
An airline printed his name in all capitals, and security rejected his boarding pass
A form cut his surname off after the first ten letters

questions.explanation:
On 17 June 2010, Graham-Cumming blogged about a website that answered "Graham-Cumming" with an error saying his last name contained invalid characters. He pointed out that the site really meant it wouldn't accept the hyphen, and that calling part of someone's name "invalid" is rude.

The bug usually comes from a validation pattern like `^[A-Za-z]+$`. It looks tidy, but it rejects hyphens, apostrophes, spaces and every letter outside basic Latin. The W3C advises name fields to accept every character people use and to validate as little as possible.
questions.references: [John Graham-Cumming: Your last name contains invalid characters (2010)](https://blog.jgc.org/2010/06/your-last-name-contains-invalid.html), [W3C: Personal names around the world](https://www.w3.org/International/questions/qa-personal-names)

questions.title: Janice "Lokelani" Keihanaikukauakahihuliheekahaunaele's surname is 36 characters long. In 2013, Hawaii's ID system allowed 35. What did her driver's licence show?

options.text: Her surname with the final letter cut off
No first name at all
Her surname abbreviated to its first ten letters
Her maiden name in place of her married name

questions.explanation:
Her surname has 35 letters plus an ʻokina, the Hawaiian glottal-stop mark, for 36 characters in total. Hawaii County's system cut it to fit the 35-character limit, and her licence and state ID left out her first name entirely. After a police officer gave her a hard time over the licence at a traffic stop, she wrote to Honolulu station KHON, and the story spread in September 2013.

The state then updated its system to allow 40 characters for first and last names, and at the end of December 2013 she got a licence with her full name.

A fixed-width name field is a guess about the longest name anyone will have. When the guess is wrong, silently cutting the name off is the worst outcome, because the card then shows a name that belongs to nobody and doesn't match her other records.
questions.references: [CBS News: Hawaii woman's last name so long it won't fit on her license (2013)](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/hawaii-womans-last-name-so-long-it-wont-fit-on-her-license/), [Fox News: Hawaii woman with long last name forces state to alter ID policy (2013)](https://www.foxnews.com/us/hawaii-woman-with-long-last-name-forces-state-to-alter-id-policy)

questions.title: Final boss: which of these assumptions about names are false?
questions.description: Every person in this Quiz ran into at least one of them.

options.text: People's names do not change
People's names fit within a certain defined amount of space
People's names are written in ASCII
People have last names, family names, or anything else shared with their relatives

questions.explanation:
All four are false. Each one paraphrases an item on McKenzie's list, and each has a real counterexample:

- **Names change.** Jennifer Null took her surname when she married, and the new name broke airline websites.
- **Names don't fit a fixed width.** Hawaii's 35-character field cut off the end of a real surname.
- **Names aren't ASCII.** Written Hawaiian uses the ʻokina and the kahakō. Most of the world's names use characters outside ASCII, and a pattern like `^[A-Za-z]+$` rejects them.
- **Not everyone has a family name.** Many Indonesians go by a single name, and Icelandic surnames are patronymics that differ between parent and child.

The fix for all of them is the same. Store a name as a Unicode string in one generous field, keep it exactly as the person typed it, and never treat it as a boolean, a missing value, a rude word or code.
questions.references: [Patrick McKenzie: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names (2010)](https://www.kalzumeus.com/2010/06/17/falsehoods-programmers-believe-about-names/), [W3C: Personal names around the world](https://www.w3.org/International/questions/qa-personal-names)
